summary: A 1970 memo presenting the new host-to-host protocol, with changes from the earlier design in RFC 11 that came out of a December 1969 network meeting. It was described as not yet detailed enough to write a network control program from. It was updated by RFC 36 and RFC 47.

eli5.summary: This note gives a newer set of rules for how two computers start, run and end a conversation, improving on the older rules.

subtitle: The 1970 paper that lays out the ARPA network's HOST-HOST protocol: sockets, connections and control commands.

tldr.problem: Very different computers and time-sharing systems on the ARPA network needed a common way for processes at one HOST to talk to processes at another, with no single node in control.
tldr.mechanism: Each HOST runs a Network Control Program (NCP) that sets up simplex connections between pairs of sockets, using control commands sent over a designated control link.
tldr.outcome: The RFC says it does not contain enough information to write an NCP. It was updated by RFC 36 and RFC 47.

today: The metadata lists RFC 33 as Unknown status and not obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 36 and RFC 47. It obsoletes RFC 11, and the RFC itself says it lacks the detail needed to write an NCP.

sections.title: The Network as Seen by Hosts
sections.content:
The memo attaches a paper for the SJCC on the HOST-HOST protocol, with changes from the older protocol in RFC 11 that came out of the December 8, 1969 network meeting. A HOST is a computer in the network. An IMP (Interface Message Processor) is a Honeywell DDP-516 that connects up to four HOSTs at a site and forms a store-and-forward network with the other IMPs.

A message is a bit stream of less than 8096 bits. Its first 32 bits are the leader, holding the HOST, message type, flags and link number. There are 256 unidirectional links between a pair of HOSTs, and only one message at a time may be on a link. After sending, the sender must wait for a RFNM (Request-for-Next-Message) from the receiving IMP before sending again on that link.
sections.eli5: Computers hand letters to a post box machine. After each letter on a given road, you must wait for a "got it" note before sending the next.

sections.title: Connections, NCPs and Sockets
sections.content:
The design philosophy preserves decentralized control of each computer, supports interactive use, avoids restrictions on character sets or languages, stays open-ended and needs minimal change to the HOST operating system.

A connection extends a link and joins two processes so one's output is the other's input. Connections are simplex, so two are needed for a two-way conversation. Processes use system calls to reach the Network Control Program (NCP), which establishes, breaks and switches connections and controls flow. NCPs talk to each other over a designated control link.

A socket is one end of a connection and is the concatenation of a 24-bit user number, an 8-bit HOST number and an 8-bit AEN. The lower-order bit of the AEN marks a receive socket (0) or a send socket (1).
sections.eli5: Each program gets numbered mailboxes. A conversation is a pair of mailboxes, one for sending and one for receiving, and each helper program arranges them.

sections.title: System Calls and Control Commands
sections.content:
The suggested system calls are Init, Listen, Accept, Close and Transmit. Control commands each start with an 8-bit operation code. RFC (Request for Connection) is sent after an Init or Accept, CLS ends a connection, CEASE tells the sender to stop on a link, and RESUME negates a previous CEASE.

Using the same command to start and to accept a connection means two processes calling each other cannot deadlock.

For logging in, a process called the logger listens on socket number 0, switches the call to a higher even-numbered socket, and calls back to the socket one less than the caller's send socket. In this way the logger can initiate 127 conversations. The paper also notes that a TELNET subsystem will let a user at one site connect to another and appear as a regular terminal user.
sections.eli5: One side says "can we talk?", the other says "yes", and either can say "slow down", "go again" or "goodbye". A greeter program answers new visitors.
